title: The bees and the honey — no juice says "I am from this tree" (6.9)
hook: bees gather nectar from many different trees, and in the honey, no drop can say which tree it came from

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep, the bird on a string coming back to where it's tied. Your line was rest is return.

Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. Bees visited clover, dandelion, an apple tree, a lime tree, and plenty of flowers no one will ever list. They brought it all home and worked it together into one golden thing. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't. It's not gone; it's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.
screen: `WILDFLOWER HONEY.` → `CLOVER, DANDELION, APPLE, LIME.` → `FIND THE APPLE-TREE PART.`

segments.voice: Just as bees make honey, my dear, Uddalaka says, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way all these creatures, when they merge into Being, in deep sleep and at death, don't know: we have merged into Being. Then a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be. Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So the honey isn't the end of the story. Hold both halves. In the depth of Being, the separate names are gone. And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. Uddalaka isn't erasing anyone's life. In his picture, underneath a name, a family, a whole history, there's one sweetness shared with everything that lives. And from the inside, no one notices the merging. A person sleeps, wakes up, and goes back to being themselves. Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.
screen: `MANY JUICES, ONE SWEETNESS.` · `NO JUICE SAYS: I'M FROM THIS TREE.` · `THE TIGER WAKES UP A TIGER.` · `TELL ME MORE, SIR.` · then, large: `THE NAMES ARE GONE IN THE HONEY.`

segments.voice: Pick out the separate sounds around you one at a time, a fan, a car outside, a voice, your own breath, and name each one. Then, breath by breath, stop naming them, and let them run together into one sound, no part saying where it came from.
Madhu, honey, sweetness. Many juices, one sweetness: in Being, no creature says I came from this tree, and in the world, each comes back as itself.
Your line: the rivers lose their names, just as the juices lose their trees. Tomorrow, those rivers. See you then.

screen: `DAY 345 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RIVERS AND THE SEA.`

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

chat.says: What's Uddalaka's point about bees and honey?
options: In Being, names merge like juices in honey; in the world, each returns as itself.
That bees are sacred, so honey should be offered at every single prayer.
That creatures know when they merge into Being, like bees know their hive.
chat.meaning: In honey, no juice says I'm from this tree; merged in Being, creatures don't know it. Yet in the world, each becomes itself again.

Uddalaka.meaning: Shvetaketu's father, a great teacher of the Upanishads

Shvetaketu.meaning: Uddalaka's son, home after twelve years of study

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'a hundred' flowers/trees (text says many) cut; narrator's 'there's one sweetness you share' and 'you can't feel the merging' reframed as Uddalaka's picture; practice changed so it no longer repeats day 340's see-past-the-label move (now sounds blending into one).
'In deep sleep and at death' is a common reading of 'when they merge into Being' here (cf. 6.8 and 6.10); the text itself says 'merge into Being'. Confirm.
Creature list (tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth/fly, gnat, mosquito) per 6.9.3; translators vary on the insect names.

Carry 'the rivers lose their names' kept exactly as the index; it anticipates tomorrow's rivers (6.10). The voice ties it to today's image without teaching 6.10. Suggest the outline use 'the juices lose their trees' for this day.
